question: A 32-year-old woman comes to her doctor’s office with abdominal distention, diffuse abdominal pain, and a history of 10–12 bowel movements a day for the last week. She was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease 3 years ago. Today, vitals are normal. Her abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender to palpation. A CT scan shows evidence of a fistula and strictures located in the last 30 cm of her ileum. A resection of the affected portion of the bowel is scheduled. What changes in bile metabolism are expected in this patient post-procedure?

options.opa: Absorption of vitamin K will not be impaired
options.opb: Synthesis of cholesterol in the liver will decrease
options.opc: The balance of the components in bile will be altered
options.opd: Enteric bacteria will remain the same in the small intestine

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Resection of the affected portion of the bowel" -> "Decreased bile acid reabsorption in the ileum" -> "Increased bile acid excretion in feces" -> 85% CHAIN: "Resection of the affected portion of the bowel" -> "Altered bile salt composition due to reduced reabsorption" -> "Changes in bile components" -> 80% CHAIN: "Resection of the affected portion of the bowel" -> "Decreased 7⍺-dehydroxylated bile acid production" -> "Reduced absorption of 7⍺-dehydroxylated bile" -> 85%
enhanced_information: After resection of the affected portion of the bowel in a patient with Crohn's disease, changes in bile metabolism are expected, including altered bile salt composition due to reduced reabsorption, leading to changes in bile components. This may result in decreased absorption of 7⍺-dehydroxylated bile, impacting bile acid excretion in feces. Therefore, the balance of the components in bile is likely to be altered post-procedure.
analysis: In patients with Crohn's disease who undergo resection of the ileum, bile acid metabolism is significantly affected. The ileum is the primary site for bile acid reabsorption. When the ileum is resected, the reabsorption of bile acids is impaired, leading to a decrease in the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids. This results in a decrease in the absorption of bile acids, including 7⍺-dehydroxylated bile acids, which are secondary bile acids formed by bacterial action in the colon. This can lead to bile acid malabsorption and subsequent diarrhea. The other options do not directly relate to the expected changes in bile metabolism post-ileal resection.
